q: "If God made everything, then who made God?"
short: Nobody made God, and that isn't a dodge. The argument for God is about things that depend on something else to exist. God is the one who doesn't depend on anything, so asking who made Him is like asking who made the thing that was never made.
why: Everything around you depends on something else: you on your parents, the rain on the clouds, the clouds on the sun.

A chain of things that all depend on something can't explain itself, even if it goes on forever. It's like a line of soldiers each waiting for permission to fire: if no one ever gives the first order, nobody fires.
So there has to be something that doesn't depend on anything. That is what Muslims mean by Allah.

push.they: "But that's just special pleading for God."
push.you: If God needed a maker, then that maker would be the independent one, and the question stops there. Something has to be independent, or nothing would exist at all.

q: "You only believe in God because your parents told you to."
short: Research on young children suggests the opposite. Kids in many countries naturally see the world as made on purpose, even when nobody teaches them. Islam calls this inborn sense the fitrah.
why: Studies of children across cultures found they naturally think nature was designed by a powerful mind.
Not believing in a Creator usually has to be learned.
The Quran says people are created with this natural sense (30:30).

push.they: "Kids also believe in Santa. A natural belief can be wrong."
push.you: True, so this alone doesn't prove God. But we trust lots of natural beliefs, like that other people have minds, unless someone shows they're false. So the person saying 'there's no God' has to show why this one is false.

q: "You don't need God to be a good person."
short: Agreed: plenty of people who don't believe in God are kind and honest. The real question is different. If there is no God, what makes something actually wrong, rather than just disliked by a lot of people?
why: Almost everyone believes some things are really wrong, like torturing a child for fun, not just 'wrong for me'.
Facts about the world, on their own, don't tell you what you ought to do.
If God exists, there is a real standard of right and wrong that doesn't change with opinion or majority.

push.they: "Morality is just what helps humans survive."
push.you: That explains why we feel things are wrong. It doesn't explain why they actually are wrong. If a society voted that cruelty was fine, would it become fine?

q: "If God is good, why is there so much suffering?"
short: This is one of the hardest questions, and it's okay to feel it. Islam's answer is that this life is a test, not the final stop, and that a God who is far wiser than us will have reasons we can't always see. Islam also promises that every wrong will be put right.
why: Suffering can lead to growth, patience and compassion, and the Quran describes life as a test.
If God is infinitely wise, we should expect not to see all of His reasons, just as a small child can't see why a parent says no.
Only if God exists will every victim finally get justice.

push.they: "What about babies with cancer? Who grows from that?"
push.you: Sometimes we honestly can't see the reason, and Islam doesn't pretend we always can. But not seeing a reason isn't the same as there being no reason. In one hadith the Prophet ﷺ saw children who had died in a garden around Abraham, and said this included the children of non-Muslims too (Sahih al-Bukhari 7047).

honest: Even very strong believers find this question painful. Talking about it with someone you trust is a good thing, not a sign of weak faith.

q: "Evolution proves there's no God."
short: Evolution is a scientific idea about how living things change. 'There is no God' is a different kind of claim, a belief about everything. Even if evolution were completely true, it wouldn't explain why there is a universe at all, why it has laws, or how life started.
why: Science describes how nature works. It can't tell you whether anything exists beyond nature.
How life first began is still unexplained by science.
Turning evolution into 'so there is no God' is philosophy, not biology.

push.they: "So you're anti-science?"
push.you: No. I'm saying the science doesn't reach the conclusion you're drawing. That's a different question.

q: "How do you know the Quran wasn't changed over the centuries?"
short: The Quran was kept in two ways at once from the very start: memorised by huge numbers of people and written down. Each one checked the other, and very early manuscripts match the Quran we read today.
why: People recited it out loud every day in prayer, so a changed word would be corrected by everyone listening.
It was written down during the Prophet's ﷺ life, gathered soon after his death, and standardised within about twenty years.
Some manuscripts have been radiocarbon-dated to around the time of the Prophet's Companions.

push.they: "Memory isn't reliable. It's like a game of telephone."
push.you: Telephone works because one person whispers to one person. The Quran was recited word for word by crowds who would correct a mistake straight away, and it was written down at the same time.

q: "There are different versions of the Quran."
short: There are different recognised ways of reciting the same Quran, called the qira'at. They come from the Prophet ﷺ himself, they affect only a small number of words, and they don't change the message.
why: The differences were taught by the Prophet ﷺ, so they are part of the Quran, not mistakes in copying it.
They share the same written outline.
People sometimes mix up three different things (the ahruf, the readings and the written text) and call them 'versions'.

push.they: "If it was perfectly kept, why are there any differences?"
push.you: Because those differences were part of how it was given. Keeping it perfectly means keeping it exactly as it was revealed, and it was revealed with them.

q: "The Quran just copied stories from the Bible and old legends."
short: The Quran tells some of the same stories because it says they come from the same God and the same prophets. When you compare closely, its versions differ in important ways, and some of the 'sources' critics name were written after the Quran.
why: Sharing a story isn't copying it. The Quran often corrects details in older versions.
Some texts that are said to be the source actually come later than the Quran.
The Quran leaves out the fantastical extras those legends contain.

push.they: "Maybe Muhammad just heard the stories from people around him."
push.you: Then you have to explain why he kept the core, corrected the theology and dropped all the made-up parts, every single time.

q: "Doesn't the Quran say the earth is flat?"
short: No. Classical Muslim scholars from different schools said there was agreement that the earth is round, and the Quran's language fits a round world.
why: Well-known classical scholars reported a consensus that the earth is a sphere.
The Quran describes night 'wrapping' around day (39:5), which fits a round earth.
When the Quran says the earth is 'spread out', it describes how a huge sphere looks from where you stand.

push.they: "But some Muslims today believe in a flat earth."
push.you: A few people's opinions don't define the text. The mainstream view of classical scholars was a round earth.

q: "Did Muhammad ﷺ even exist?"
short: Yes. People who were not Muslim, including Christian writers, mentioned him within a few decades of his death. They described a prophet among the Arabs who preached the God of Abraham.
why: Non-Muslim writers from that time describe him and what he taught.
Coins and inscriptions from the early period back this up.
Historians today, including non-Muslims, don't seriously doubt that he existed.

push.they: "Islamic sources were written much later."
push.you: That's why the outside sources matter. People who didn't follow him, and some who opposed him, still wrote about him early on.

q: "How do we know Muhammad ﷺ wasn't just making it all up?"
short: Look at how he behaved when lying would have helped him. On the day his son died, there was an eclipse and people said the sky was mourning. He publicly said no, eclipses don't happen because someone died. A fake prophet would have taken that free 'miracle'.
why: He turned down a sign that would have made him look more powerful.
The Quran even corrects him in places, which a self-promoter wouldn't write.
He refused wealth and power when they were offered to him.

push.they: "Being sincere doesn't make you right."
push.you: True. This only shows he wasn't a liar. Then you have to ask whether he was sincere but mistaken, and look at everything else: the Quran itself, the prophecies and his life.

q: "He just used religion to get power and money."
short: His life shows the opposite. While he ruled Arabia he slept on a reed mat, and his family were not allowed to take charity money.
why: He lived simply even when he had power.
He banned his own family from receiving zakat (charity).
He prayed at night until his feet swelled. That isn't how someone acting for personal gain spends his nights.

push.they: "Maybe he wanted fame, not money."
push.you: Then why did he turn down the worldly offers made to him, and keep reciting verses that corrected him in public?

q: "What's so special about the Quran anyway?"
short: The Quran challenged the best Arabic speakers of its time to produce even one short chapter like it. They hated the Prophet ﷺ and had every reason to try. They chose to fight him instead.
why: The challenge was public and the bar was low: just one chapter.
The people who heard it were the experts in Arabic poetry and speech.
Even its enemies said it was unlike any kind of speech they knew.

push.they: "Every great writer is unique. Shakespeare is too."
push.you: Shakespeare never said 'nobody can match this, try it'. The Quran did, to people who wanted to prove it wrong, and the form it uses fits none of the known kinds of Arabic speech.

q: "The hadith were written 200 years after the Prophet ﷺ, so you can't trust them."
short: Some hadith were being written down while the Prophet ﷺ was still alive. Collections like Bukhari came later, but they were built from earlier writing and memorisation, not invented from nothing.
why: Abu Huraira said that Abdullah ibn Amr used to write hadith down (Sahih al-Bukhari 113).
The Prophet ﷺ told Abdullah ibn Amr to write, saying 'only truth comes out of it' (Sunan Abi Dawud 3646).
When a man asked for a speech to be written for him, the Prophet ﷺ said 'Write it for Abu Shah' (Sahih al-Bukhari 2434).

push.they: "But Muslim 3004 says don't write anything except the Quran."
push.you: Read the whole hadith. It goes on: 'and narrate from me, there is no harm'. And other hadith show writing was allowed. Scholars explain the first part in different ways, but it can't mean nothing was ever written.

q: "Some hadith are fake, so how can you trust any of them?"
short: Muslim scholars knew some reports were fake, and they built a careful system to check them. They looked at who passed each report on and whether its content made sense.
why: Scholars graded each report by checking the people who passed it on: were they honest, and did they remember well?
They even questioned reports in the most respected collections.
Spotting fakes is a sign the system was taken seriously, not a reason to throw everything out.

push.they: "Muslims just call the hadith they don't like 'weak'."
push.you: These gradings were made centuries ago by scholars with no stake in today's arguments, using the same rules for every report, even ones Muslims like.

q: "Why not just follow the Quran and ignore hadith?"
short: Because the Quran itself tells us to follow the Prophet ﷺ, and you can't actually practise Islam without his example. Try to pray using only the Quran: it doesn't tell you how many units, or exactly what to say.
why: The Quran tells believers to obey the Messenger, not just the Book.
It calls him the one who explains the revelation (16:44).
The details of prayer and charity come from his example (the Sunnah).

push.they: "The Quran says 'We have left out nothing from the Book'."
push.you: Many scholars say 'the Book' there means the Preserved Tablet. Even if it means the Quran, the Quran includes the command to follow the Prophet, so it leaves nothing out by sending us to him.

q: "Islam treats women as less than men."
short: In Islam men and women are equal in worth, in reward from God and in responsibility. They are given some different roles, and different doesn't have to mean unequal.
why: The Quran speaks to men and women side by side and promises them the same reward (33:35, 16:97).
God judges people by their character, not their gender (49:13).
A woman's money is fully her own, while a husband must provide for the family.

push.they: "'Equal but different' is just an excuse."
push.you: It's only unfair if the difference is random or one-sided. Here each role comes with matching duties. And we already accept some differences as fair, like separate sports leagues.

q: "Why do Muslim girls have to wear a hijab?"
short: The Quran asks believing women to cover their hair and body in public. It gives the reason as dignity and protection from harassment (33:59). Covering was also normal in Jewish and Christian tradition for a long time.
why: It comes from the Quran (24:31 and 33:59).
Its stated purpose is respect and safety, not shame.
Many Christian and Jewish women covered too, and some still do.

push.they: "Nobody should tell women what to wear."
push.you: Every society has some rules about clothing, even if they're about showing less rather than more. The real question is what the rule is based on. Mine is based on what God revealed.

q: "What about Aisha's age?"
short: The authentic reports say Aisha was six at the marriage contract and nine when the marriage began. In the ancient world, marriage around puberty was normal in many cultures, including Jewish and Christian ones. Nobody at the time, including the Prophet's ﷺ enemies, objected. Aisha grew up to be one of the greatest scholars in Islam.
why: Marriage soon after puberty was common across the ancient and medieval world.
The marriage began after she had reached physical maturity, with her family's agreement.
His enemies attacked him on many things, but never on this.

push.they: "It was wrong then and it's wrong now."
push.you: Islam agrees harm is always wrong, and Islamic law forbids marriages that cause harm. But the age people married at has always depended on maturity and on society. If marriage at 12 or 13 was always evil, most of our ancestors, in every religion, were in evil marriages.

honest: Some people say she was 19, but that rests on weak evidence. It's better to know the real reports and the context than to rely on an argument that falls apart when checked.

q: "Islam allowed slavery."
short: Slavery existed almost everywhere when Islam came. Islam didn't invent it. It closed most of the ways people became slaves, opened many ways out, and made freeing slaves an act of worship. The direction was towards freedom.
why: It banned enslaving free people.
Freeing a slave was a way to make up for many sins.
If a master hit a slave, the slave was to be set free (Sahih Muslim 1657).

push.they: "Why didn't it just ban slavery straight away?"
push.you: No society anywhere abolished slavery on a large scale until the 1700s and 1800s. Islam did what changed things most in the 600s: cut off the supply and open the exits.

q: "Does Islam say people who leave should be killed?"
short: Honest answer: most classical Muslim scholars held that someone who publicly leaves Islam faces the death penalty, but only after being invited to reconsider, and only decided by a court. Some scholars, early and modern, disagree. No individual is ever allowed to punish anyone.
why: The Quran says 'there is no compulsion in religion' (2:256) and sets no earthly punishment for leaving.
The classical ruling comes from hadith and was connected to publicly leaving and turning against the community.
Today scholars debate whether and how it applies, and in a non-Muslim country no Muslim may punish anyone.

push.they: "So you'd kill someone for changing their mind?"
push.you: No individual is allowed to do anything like that. Private belief was never investigated. And the ruling is debated among scholars. I'd rather tell you the accurate position than pretend it doesn't exist.

honest: This is a genuinely difficult topic. It's okay to say it's hard, and to ask a scholar you trust.

q: "Religion causes most wars."
short: The history doesn't support that. Only a small share of wars are classed as religious, and the biggest killings of the last century were carried out by non-religious governments. Groups that kill civilians in Islam's name break Islam's own rules.
why: Most wars have been about land, power and money.
The deadliest regimes of the 20th century were secular.
The Quran treats killing one innocent person like killing all of humanity (5:32).

push.they: "What about ISIS?"
push.you: Condemn them clearly. They break the Quran's rules and the Prophet's rules in war, and most of their victims were Muslims.

q: "If people are born gay, how can Islam say it's wrong?"
short: Islam separates a feeling from an action. Everyone has desires they didn't choose and are asked to control in some way. Islam treats those feelings as part of a test, not as something that makes a person bad. Treat everyone with kindness and respect while being clear about what you believe.
why: Being born with a feeling doesn't by itself decide whether acting on it is right.
Every believer is asked to hold back some desires, for example about relationships outside marriage.
The Quran says God never puts more on a person than they can bear (2:286).

push.they: "Why would God make someone a way and then forbid it?"
push.you: The same question applies to anyone asked to hold back a strong desire. Islam's answer is that life is a test and holding back is rewarded.

honest: This is personal for many people, so be gentle. Disagreeing with an action is not the same as disliking a person.
